promptText: The chapter argues caching is 'the single highest-leverage lever' for cutting both cost and latency at once. What makes it different from most other optimizations, which typically force a trade-off between the two?
options: A cache hit is both cheaper to serve (less backend compute and database load) and faster to return than redoing the original work, so the same change improves both dimensions simultaneously instead of trading one for the other
Caching only improves latency; any cost savings are a coincidental side effect of running fewer servers
Caching only reduces infrastructure cost; the extra lookup it requires actually makes every request slightly slower
Caching eliminates the need for a database entirely, so cost and latency both drop to zero
explanation: Because serving a stored answer skips expensive recomputation entirely, a cache hit is simultaneously cheaper to serve and faster to return, so a single change improves cost and latency together rather than spending one to gain the other, unlike most optimizations that trade along that axis.

promptText: Why does the chapter single out cache invalidation, rather than population or placement, as the genuinely hard sub-problem of caching?
options: A cache lives outside the one system of record that writes go to, so every write path capable of changing the underlying data must independently notify every cache holding a stale copy — missing even one leaves readers silently wrong with no error or signal
Invalidation is hard only because most caching libraries fail to expose a delete or evict API
Invalidation is actually the easiest sub-problem; the chapter ranks placement as hardest because it requires choosing among four layers
Invalidation is hard strictly because TTLs cannot be configured below one second on most caching systems
explanation: Because a cache is a second copy of the truth maintained outside the source of record, keeping it correct depends on every write path remembering to notify it; miss one path and that data silently goes stale with no exception or signal, which is exactly why invalidation earns the chapter's 'hard problem' reputation over population or placement.

promptText: In the cache-aside pattern, who is responsible for populating the cache on a miss and invalidating it on a write, and what does that cost the team?
options: The application itself owns both responsibilities at every call site, which keeps the cache technology simple (a plain key-value store) but means the miss-fill and invalidation logic must be correctly repeated everywhere the data is read or written
The cache itself owns both responsibilities via a configured loader, so the application never has to write any caching logic at all
The underlying database owns invalidation automatically through triggers, and the application only owns population
Cache-aside requires no population or invalidation step because entries in this pattern never expire
explanation: Cache-aside's defining trait is that the application checks the cache, fills it on a miss, and explicitly invalidates it on a write, which needs no special cache infrastructure but puts the burden of correctly repeating that contract on every call site touching the data, unlike read-through which centralizes the miss-fill logic inside the cache via a loader.

promptText: Why does write-through caching eliminate the 'forgot to invalidate' class of bugs that cache-aside is exposed to?
options: Every write goes to the cache first, and the cache synchronously forwards it to the underlying store before acknowledging, so a successful write guarantees both are updated and can never disagree, at the cost of higher write latency
Write-through skips writing to the cache entirely and writes only to the database, so there is nothing left to invalidate
Write-through uses the same TTL-based expiration mechanism as cache-aside, just configured with a shorter default TTL
Write-through is immune to this bug class because it never allows reads to be served from the cache, only from the database
explanation: Because write-through makes the cache responsible for synchronously writing through to the store before the write is considered complete, the two can never end up disagreeing after a successful write; the trade is that every write now pays for both the cache write and the store write before returning, unlike cache-aside where a missed invalidation call can leave a stale entry behind.

promptText: Why is TTL-based expiration described as a 'blunt instrument' compared to event-driven invalidation?
options: A TTL expires a cached entry purely based on elapsed time regardless of whether the data actually changed, so data that changed the instant after being cached stays wrong for the full TTL window, while unchanged data gets needlessly re-fetched the moment the TTL elapses
TTLs require every write path to explicitly call an eviction function, which is harder to maintain correctly than event-driven invalidation
TTL-based caches cannot be combined with any other invalidation strategy within the same system
A TTL only applies to data stored at a CDN and has no equivalent mechanism for an application-level cache
explanation: Because TTL expiration fires purely on a clock rather than reacting to an actual data change, it can leave genuinely stale data served for the full window or needlessly discard data that never changed, whereas event-driven invalidation reacts immediately to the write itself at the cost of requiring every write path to participate correctly.

promptText: A CDN with many edge PoPs but no origin shield is exposed to what specific failure mode when a globally popular item's cache entry expires?
options: Every edge PoP that misses locally fetches from the origin independently, so the origin can receive one simultaneous request per PoP worldwide for content that only needed to be fetched once — the flash-crowd problem relocated one layer inward
The CDN automatically falls back to serving the item from the requesting client's own browser cache instead of the origin
All edge PoPs become permanently unable to cache that item again until the CDN provider is manually reconfigured
The origin receives zero requests because edge PoPs silently drop requests for content whose entry has expired
explanation: Without a shield, each edge PoP independently treats its own local miss as a first-time fetch, so a popular item's expiration can trigger one origin request per PoP simultaneously, exactly the flash-crowd problem CDNs exist to prevent, just moved one layer inward; an origin shield collapses this to at most one request per cache-lifetime by being the only layer allowed to talk to the origin directly.

promptText: Among locking/request coalescing and stale-while-revalidate, what is the key behavioral difference in how a waiting client experiences a cache stampede on a hot key?
options: Locking and coalescing make concurrent requests wait or retry for the one in-flight regeneration to finish, while stale-while-revalidate never makes any request wait — it returns the just-expired value immediately and triggers exactly one background refresh
Locking returns stale data immediately to every requester, while stale-while-revalidate forces every request to wait for a freshly regenerated value
All three techniques behave identically from the client's perspective and differ only in which backing store they protect
Coalescing and stale-while-revalidate both require the client to manually retry, while locking is fully transparent to the client
explanation: Locking and request coalescing resolve the stampede by having concurrent requests wait on, or retry after, a single in-flight regeneration, whereas stale-while-revalidate avoids any wait entirely by serving the just-expired value right away and performing the one necessary refresh in the background, at the cost of briefly serving known-stale data.

promptText: Using blended_latency = (hit_ratio × cache_latency) + (miss_ratio × origin_latency) with cache_latency = 2ms and origin_latency = 200ms, why does pushing the hit ratio from 90% to 99% improve latency disproportionately more than the nine-percentage-point change alone suggests?
options: The miss_ratio term dominates the formula because origin_latency is so much larger than cache_latency, so cutting miss_ratio tenfold (0.1 to 0.01) removes most of that dominant term, dropping blended latency from 21.8ms to 3.98ms, a much larger jump than the percentage-point change implies
Blended latency is actually independent of hit_ratio once it exceeds 90%, so the improvement is purely an artifact of rounding
Cache_latency increases non-linearly as hit_ratio rises, which cancels out most of the expected improvement
The formula only applies below a 90% hit ratio; above that, origin_latency alone must be used
explanation: Because origin_latency (200ms) vastly exceeds cache_latency (2ms), the miss_ratio term drives most of the blended-latency value even at a seemingly high hit ratio, so shrinking miss_ratio tenfold from 0.1 to 0.01 produces a much larger latency win than the modest-looking jump from 90% to 99% suggests on its own.

promptText: A system has a 70% CDN hit ratio and an 80% application-cache hit ratio. Per the chapter's multiplicative model, what fraction of original traffic reaches the database, and what does this imply about layered caching strategy?
options: (1 − 0.7) × (1 − 0.8) = 0.06, so only about 6% of original traffic reaches the database — each layer only needs to be moderately effective on its own for the combination to be highly effective
0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56, so 56% of traffic reaches the database, meaning layering two caches barely helps
The two ratios cannot be combined mathematically; only the single higher ratio of 80% determines database load
1 − (0.7 + 0.8) = -0.5, meaning the database effectively receives negative traffic, which only request coalescing can produce
explanation: Hit ratios at successive layers multiply together via their respective miss ratios, so a 70% CDN hit ratio combined with an 80% application-cache hit ratio leaves (1-0.7) × (1-0.8) = 6% of traffic for the database, which is the quantitative reason the chapter argues for moderately effective caching at multiple layers rather than one layer pushed toward an extreme.

promptText: A shared CDN cache key for a personalized API response fails to account for the user's auth cookie. What is the direct consequence, and which header is responsible for preventing it?
options: One user's personalized response can be cached under a key that a different user subsequently requests and receives, a serious confidentiality failure; the Vary header is what tells a shared cache which request inputs must be folded into the cache key
The response simply bypasses the CDN entirely and is always fetched fresh from the origin, which is slow but safe
The Cache-Control header alone, regardless of Vary, fully prevents this scenario as long as max-age is set to a nonzero value
This only affects browser caches, never shared CDN caches, since CDNs ignore auth cookies by design
explanation: If the cache key doesn't capture every input the response actually varies on, here the auth cookie, the CDN computes the same key for requests that should produce different responses and can serve one user's personalized data to another; the Vary header is exactly what tells a shared cache which additional request headers must be factored into the cache key to prevent this.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend a separate, shorter TTL for cached error responses or empty results rather than reusing the TTL used for successful responses?
options: Applying a long TTL meant for successful responses to a transient failure can turn a brief blip into a sustained outage, since the cached negative result keeps being served long after the underlying condition has actually cleared
Error responses cannot be cached at all under any TTL, so the question of TTL length does not apply to them
A shorter TTL for errors is purely a performance optimization with no correctness implication
Negative caching is only relevant at the browser layer and never at the application or CDN layer
explanation: A long TTL applied to an error or empty result means that cached negative outcome keeps being served well past the point the real condition recovered, extending what should have been a brief blip into a sustained, self-inflicted outage; a deliberately short, separate TTL for negative results lets the system recover quickly once the underlying issue clears.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue cache sizing conversations should focus on 'does the working set fit' rather than 'does the entire dataset fit'?
options: Real access patterns are typically Zipf-skewed, so a small fraction of keys account for a disproportionate share of requests; an LRU/LFU eviction policy approximates holding just that popular working set, making a cache far smaller than the full dataset sufficient for a high hit ratio
Modern caches always have enough memory to hold any dataset, so sizing conversations are purely theoretical
The entire dataset must always fit in the cache, or the hit-ratio formula from the chapter's mathematics section becomes invalid
Working set size is unrelated to popularity; it is determined solely by the number of distinct tables in the database
explanation: Because access patterns rarely are uniform and tend to follow a Zipf-like skew, only a comparatively small set of currently-popular keys needs to be resident for a high hit ratio, and LRU/LFU eviction approximates exactly that working set without needing to know the popularity distribution in advance, so over-provisioning for the whole dataset spends money an eviction policy was already making unnecessary.

promptText: A method annotated @Cacheable is called from another method on the same Spring bean via `this`, and production shows it still hits the database on every call despite identical arguments. What is the most likely cause, and why does it have nothing to do with cache configuration?
options: Spring's caching annotations work through a dynamic proxy wrapping the bean; a call made via `this` instead of through the proxy bypasses that interception entirely, so the method body runs directly and caching is silently skipped regardless of how the cache provider is configured
The cache provider, Redis or Caffeine, must be misconfigured, since @Cacheable always works correctly for same-class method calls
@Cacheable requires the calling method to also be annotated @Cacheable, or caching is disabled transitively for the whole bean
Self-invocation triggers an automatic cache eviction on every call, which is a deliberate Spring safety feature
explanation: Because Spring implements @Cacheable via an AOP proxy around the bean, only calls that go through that proxy are intercepted; a same-bean call via `this` invokes the real method directly and never passes through the proxy, so caching is silently skipped, a classic gotcha that stems from how Spring AOP proxies work rather than from cache provider misconfiguration.

promptText: Why does the chapter treat access control on a CDN's purge API as a security concern rather than just an operational one?
options: An attacker, or an overly-permissive internal tool, able to trigger arbitrary purges can force a flood of cache misses to hit the origin directly, effectively weaponizing the cache-invalidation mechanism itself as a denial-of-service vector against the origin
Purge APIs can only add new entries to a cache, so misuse at worst causes excessive memory consumption rather than origin load
Purge access control matters solely to prevent accidental billing overages from the CDN provider, with no availability impact
CDN purge APIs are inherently read-only and therefore cannot affect what traffic the origin receives
explanation: Because purging deletes cache entries and forces subsequent requests to miss and reach the origin, uncontrolled purge access lets an attacker or misconfigured tool turn the cache-invalidation mechanism into a tool for flooding the origin with traffic it would otherwise never see, the same mechanism meant to keep data fresh becoming a denial-of-service lever if left unprotected.

promptText: Despite having both an origin shield and stale-while-revalidate configured at the CDN, a viral piece of brand-new content still causes a brief, single consolidated request to the origin the moment its entry first needs to be fetched. Does this indicate either protection failed?
options: No — the shield guarantees at most one origin fetch per unique content per shield-cache-lifetime, and stale-while-revalidate only helps once a prior value exists to serve stale; on a true first-time fetch there is nothing stale yet to serve, so one consolidated request to origin is the expected, bounded behavior
Yes, this proves the origin shield is completely ineffective and should be replaced with direct per-PoP origin access
Yes, this means stale-while-revalidate must be disabled, since it is fundamentally incompatible with origin shielding
No — this request is actually the database being hit directly, unrelated to either CDN protection, since CDNs cannot shield genuinely new content
explanation: An origin shield bounds concurrent origin fetches to at most one per shield-cache-lifetime regardless of how many edge PoPs ask, and that one consolidated fetch is exactly what's expected on a true first-time miss, since stale-while-revalidate has no previously-cached value to serve until after that first fetch populates the shield, so a single bounded request at first-fetch time is correct behavior, not evidence either mechanism failed.
